PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 86 — Lesson 110: Skin Cancer & Suspicious Lesion Management

FNP-level goal: Evaluate a changing or suspicious lesion in its clinical context, use morphology and risk factors to decide who needs timely tissue diagnosis or dermatology care, distinguish patient-specific evaluation from population-screening claims, and create a closed-loop plan that does not lose a potentially malignant lesion to follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish evaluation of a symptomatic or changing lesion from routine population skin-cancer screening.
  • Describe concerning features of melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, and actinic keratosis without treating an acronym as a diagnosis.
  • Perform and document a focused lesion and risk assessment across all skin tones.
  • Recognize when biopsy or dermatology referral is safer than empiric destruction, reassurance, or serial observation.
  • Apply prevention counseling, photo documentation, referral tracking, and urgent eye or systemic red-flag disposition.

Part 1 — A Changing Lesion Is a Clinical Problem

Population recommendations about routine whole-body skin examination do not answer the question raised by a patient who has a new, changing, bleeding, painful, nonhealing, or otherwise suspicious lesion. The FNP is not deciding whether every asymptomatic adult needs the same screening interval. The FNP is deciding whether this person’s lesion and risk context need tissue diagnosis, expert examination, close documented surveillance, or urgent escalation.

Begin with the patient’s concern. Ask when the lesion first appeared; whether it has changed in size, shape, color, texture, symptoms, or bleeding; whether it heals and returns; whether it differs from the patient’s other lesions; and whether a family member noticed evolution. A lesion that is new or evolving in adulthood deserves attention even when it is small, painless, or on a less visible site.

Part 2 — Cancer Biology Explains the Clinical Clues

Skin cancers arise through different pathways, but all require the FNP to respect progressive growth and local or metastatic potential. Ultraviolet exposure, intermittent severe sunburns, cumulative exposure, tanning devices, immunosuppression, prior skin cancer, certain genetic or family histories, and lighter or easily burning skin can increase risk. However, cancer can occur in every skin tone and in areas with limited sun exposure. A lower perceived risk must not become delayed assessment.

Melanoma can arise from a preexisting nevus or de novo and may be pigmented, amelanotic, or subtly different from surrounding lesions. Basal cell carcinoma often appears as a pearly, translucent, ulcerated, or persistently bleeding papule or plaque, but varies by skin tone and site. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma may appear as a persistent scaly, crusted, tender, hyperkeratotic, or nonhealing lesion; risk is higher in chronic sun damage, certain wounds or scars, and immunosuppression. Actinic keratoses are rough, scaly, sun-damaged lesions that signal cumulative exposure and merit a plan, but they are not interchangeable with invasive cancer.

Part 3 — The Morphology Framework: Describe Before You Diagnose

Document the lesion type, size in millimeters, color or colors, symmetry, border, surface, scale, ulceration, bleeding, induration, tenderness, fixation, and exact anatomic site. For pigmented lesions, the ABCDE framework—Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter or Darkening, and Evolution—can prompt questions, but no one element rules melanoma in or out. The ugly-duckling concept is often useful: a lesion that looks meaningfully different from the patient’s other nevi deserves attention even if it does not satisfy every ABCDE feature.

In darker skin, erythema may be less visible and pigmented lesions may occur on palms, soles, nail units, mucosa, or other areas that are overlooked in a sun-exposure-only mental model. Examine the specific lesion and related regional skin; a broader examination is guided by concern, patient risk, consent, and setting. Do not dismiss acral, nail, or mucosal changes because the patient does not fit a stereotyped high-risk profile.

Part 4 — Focused Risk History

Ask about personal history of melanoma or nonmelanoma skin cancer, prior biopsies, family history of melanoma or pancreatic cancer when relevant, atypical nevi, blistering sunburns, tanning-device use, occupational and recreational ultraviolet exposure, immunosuppressive medications or transplant history, radiation, chronic wounds, and difficulty visualizing the area. Ask whether the patient is pregnant, anticoagulated, immunocompromised, or has a healing disorder if a procedural pathway is being considered.

Risk factors influence urgency and follow-up, but they do not replace morphology. A low-risk patient with a bleeding nonhealing lesion may still need timely evaluation; a high-risk patient with a clearly benign stable lesion may still need appropriate surveillance rather than panic. Good reasoning combines lesion behavior with patient context.

Part 5 — Differential Diagnosis and Diagnostic Boundaries

Common benign mimics include seborrheic keratosis, dermatofibroma, nevus, lentigo, angioma, wart, inflammatory lesions, scars, and benign cysts. Inflammation, trauma, infection, or medication reactions can alter a lesion’s appearance. Yet a benign-looking label should be earned through a coherent history and examination. Repeatedly freezing, shaving, or prescribing topical therapy for a lesion that is evolving or uncertain can delay diagnosis and complicate later pathology.

The safest next step is sometimes not a definitive diagnosis in primary care; it is a timely biopsy pathway or dermatology referral. Choose biopsy type and urgency according to lesion features, location, suspected diagnosis, procedural competence, patient factors, and local practice standards. Do not attempt destructive treatment of a lesion with a meaningful melanoma concern before obtaining an appropriate diagnostic plan.

Part 6 — When Referral Is Time-Sensitive

Arrange timely dermatology or procedural evaluation for a changing pigmented lesion, a lesion suspicious for melanoma, a persistent nonhealing ulcer or nodule, recurrent spontaneous bleeding, induration, a lesion on a high-risk or cosmetically sensitive site, unexplained nail pigmentation or nail-unit change, an immunocompromised patient with a suspicious lesion, or a lesion that remains diagnostically uncertain after assessment. The needed time frame depends on suspected diagnosis and evolution; document the reason for urgency.

Urgent evaluation is particularly important for ocular or periocular symptoms, rapidly enlarging masses, significant infection or hemorrhage, or systemic symptoms that could indicate advanced disease. A painful changing lesion with regional nodes is not a routine annual skin-check question. The FNP’s responsibility is to recognize a possible cancer pathway and close the loop on access—not to wait indefinitely for a lesion to declare itself.

Part 7 — Prevention Without False Reassurance

Prevention counseling includes shade, protective clothing, broad-spectrum sunscreen used as directed, avoiding intentional tanning and tanning devices, and routine awareness of one’s own changing lesions. Prevention is not a promise that cancer will not occur, and sunscreen counseling must not replace evaluation of a concerning lesion. Encourage patients to seek assessment for a new or changing lesion rather than to self-diagnose from an online image.

For people with prior skin cancer, strong family history, high nevus burden, immunosuppression, or other risk factors, coordinate an individualized surveillance plan with dermatology. Document outside pathology, prior lesions, and follow-up date. A referral that is placed but never completed is not completed care.

Part 8 — Documentation and Closed-Loop Follow-Up

High-quality documentation includes the patient’s history of change, risk factors, lesion description, size, site, assessment uncertainty, clinical photograph when consented and secure systems permit, differential, plan, urgency, and explicit return precautions. If referring, identify the service, clinical question, expected time frame, and how the office will confirm completion. Review pathology or specialist recommendations directly; do not assume no news means benign news.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Changing Mole

A 48-year-old reports that a dark lesion on the upper back has become larger and now has multiple colors. It is different from other nevi and a partner recently noticed the change. The FNP documents size, morphology, evolution, and risk history, avoids destructive treatment, and arranges a timely diagnostic evaluation. The key lesson is that evolution and an ugly-duckling lesion outweigh the false reassurance of no pain.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Nonhealing Crusted Papule

An older outdoor worker has a scaly crusted papule on the ear that repeatedly bleeds when toweling and has not healed over several months. The FNP recognizes that persistent bleeding and nonhealing behavior require a cancer-focused pathway, not repeated empiric topical antibiotic treatment. Examination and referral are documented with a clear follow-up plan.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Dark Streak in a Nail

A patient with dark skin presents with a new widening pigmented streak in a thumbnail and pigment change around the nail unit. The FNP does not dismiss the finding as a common benign nail variation based on skin tone or absence of sun exposure. The change warrants prompt specialist evaluation because nail-unit lesions require careful assessment.

FNP High-Yield Framework: LESION

  1. L — Listen for evolution: new, changing, bleeding, painful, nonhealing, or different-from-others history.
  2. E — Examine and measure: morphology, size, site, color, border, surface, regional findings, and skin-tone variation.
  3. S — Stratify risk: personal and family history, ultraviolet exposure, immunosuppression, prior lesions, and difficult-to-see sites.
  4. I — Identify uncertainty: suspicious or uncertain lesions need biopsy-capable evaluation, not repeated empirical destruction.
  5. O — Organize referral: specify urgency, communicate the clinical question, and track completion and pathology.
  6. N — Navigate prevention: counsel on ultraviolet protection and self-awareness without dismissing a current concern.

Take-Home Summary

Suspicious-lesion management is not memorizing one melanoma acronym. It is a disciplined process: identify change, describe objectively, consider risk and morphology across all skin tones, avoid treatments that delay diagnosis, refer or biopsy appropriately, and verify that the diagnostic loop closes. A patient with a concerning lesion deserves an active plan even when population-level screening evidence is limited.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace dermatologic examination, dermoscopy, pathology, procedural training, current guidelines, or individualized specialist advice. A rapidly changing, bleeding, nonhealing, painful, ocular, nail-unit, or otherwise suspicious lesion requires timely clinical evaluation.
